opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most interesting and under-explored questions in the field right now. What we've seen with deep learning is basically that a set of ideas from the '60s, '70s and '80s, backpropagation, multilayer perceptrons, convolutional nets, turned out to be enormously powerful once you threw a few orders of magnitude more data and compute at them. People dismissed neural nets for decades because they didn't work well on the hardware of the time, and it turned out the problem wasn't the ideas, it was the scale.

So the natural question is: why would neural nets be the only old idea that benefits from that kind of scaling? I don't think they are. Evolutionary learning, genetic algorithms, genetic programming, probabilistic logic systems, various forms of symbolic reasoning, these were also all hobbled by the compute available when they were first developed. Genetic programming in particular was always very compute-hungry. You're evolving populations of programs, evaluating fitness over and over, and in the '90s you just couldn't run populations large enough or for enough generations to see what it could really do. I suspect if you put the kind of resources into evolutionary program learning that have gone into transformers, you'd see some quite surprising results, especially for things like creativity and generating genuinely novel structures, which is exactly where current LLMs are weakest. LLMs are great at recombining and interpolating what's in their training data, but they're not so good at the kind of open-ended, wild exploration that evolution is very good at.

Where I think it gets really exciting, though, is not running genetic algorithms on their own at massive scale, but combining them with other methods. That's a lot of what we're doing in OpenCog Hyperon. You can use neural models to guide evolutionary search, so the LLM or the neural net suggests promising regions of program space, and evolution explores around them. You can use probabilistic logic to reason about which candidate programs are worth evaluating, so you're not doing blind fitness evaluation on everything. And evolution can come up with novel structures that then get abstracted and fed back into the knowledge base. In that kind of integrated cognitive architecture, each method covers for the weaknesses of the others.

The issue is partly sociological and economic, frankly. Once deep learning started working at scale, the big tech companies poured basically all their resources into that one paradigm, because it was delivering commercial results. So there's a sort of path dependence. Nobody has done the equivalent of a GPT-scale experiment with evolutionary program learning or large-scale probabilistic logic, not because anyone has shown they wouldn't work, but because no one has paid for it. My guess is that some of these older approaches, scaled up and hybridized with neural nets, will be a big part of how we actually get from where we are now to real AGI, because I don't think just scaling up transformers on its own is going to get us there.

r001.rationale: The response argues that several older methods could benefit from more compute, but it does not claim that a high proportion of historical AI paradigms would probably work if scaled up.

r002.rationale: It says 1990s computers limited genetic programming populations, but gives no Goertzel estimate or claim that optimal population sizes were orders of magnitude beyond what those computers could support.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, actually, because I've been in the field long enough to remember when neural nets were considered a dead end, and I remember the period when genetic algorithms and genetic programming were sort of the hot thing, and then they fell out of fashion. And I think the honest answer is that the deep learning revolution was not really a victory of one idea over another idea on intellectual merits. It was a victory of one idea that happened to be well matched to the hardware that showed up, which was GPUs. Backpropagation on big matrices maps beautifully onto GPUs, and so deep learning got to ride that wave while a lot of other approaches sat there starved for compute.

Now, evolutionary methods are interesting because they're embarrassingly parallel in a way that gradient descent is not. You've got a population, you evaluate the fitness of every individual independently, and that's trivially distributable. So in principle, if you threw the kind of compute that goes into training a frontier language model at a well-designed evolutionary system, you could do some very interesting things. And we've actually seen hints of this. OpenAI did that work years ago showing evolution strategies could compete with reinforcement learning on some benchmarks if you just scaled them across enough cores. Ken Stanley and Jeff Clune's work on open-endedness and quality diversity is another example where the ideas are really powerful and have been compute-limited.

But I want to be careful here, because I don't think the right framing is "let's take the 1995 version of genetic programming and just make it bigger." Scaling a weak method gets you a bigger weak method. What I think is actually promising is hybridization. Evolution is very good at exploring structure, at discovering architectures, at finding things you didn't know to look for. Gradient descent is very good at fine-tuning parameters within a fixed structure. Those are complementary strengths. In OpenCog Hyperon, for example, we've had evolutionary learning as one of several cognitive algorithms operating on a shared knowledge representation alongside probabilistic reasoning and neural components, and the point is that each of them can help the others out of their respective ruts.

The other thing I'd say is that evolution gets really interesting when you let it operate on the learning algorithms themselves rather than just on solutions. Evolving the architectures, evolving the training procedures, evolving the representations. That's closer to what biological evolution actually did. It didn't evolve a solution to a specific problem, it evolved a brain that can learn solutions to problems. So if you ask where I'd put a lot of compute, it would be on that kind of meta-level search rather than on brute-force evolution of program trees for individual tasks.

So, in short, I think the potential is substantial and underexplored, I think a lot of the dismissal of these methods was really a historical accident of hardware, but I also think the real payoff comes from integrating them into a broader cognitive architecture rather than from treating them as a standalone competitor to deep learning.

r001.rationale: The response argues that evolutionary methods have substantial potential with more compute, but does not suggest that a high proportion of historical AI paradigms would probably work if scaled up.

r002.rationale: It gives no 1990s estimate by Goertzel of optimal genetic algorithm population sizes or comparison with contemporary computer capacity.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential there, but it depends on what you expect more computing power to buy you. With a genetic algorithm, you generate a population of candidate solutions, evaluate them, then mutate and recombine them. More compute lets you explore a much larger population and run many more generations. That can make something that was impractical thirty years ago quite useful today.

But the representation and the fitness function matter enormously. What are you evolving, and how do you tell whether it’s getting better? If every candidate is a complex program that has to interact with an environment for a long time before you can evaluate it, the computational cost can still be tremendous. And if your representation makes useful changes unlikely, you can spend a lot of compute getting nowhere.

What interests me especially is combining evolutionary search with other forms of learning and reasoning. A neural network might learn patterns that guide the search, while a reasoning system supplies structure, and evolution explores possibilities that neither would readily discover on its own.

So I wouldn’t dismiss an approach because it’s old. Some older ideas were constrained by the hardware available when they were developed. But I also wouldn’t assume that adding a million times more compute automatically turns a genetic algorithm into a generally intelligent mind. You still need the right organization of the system.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a lot of potential there. Genetic algorithms are a very general way of searching a space of possible solutions. You generate some candidates, evaluate them, keep the better ones, mutate and recombine them, and repeat. With more computing power, you can explore a much larger space. But the interesting question is whether you’ve organized that space so that useful solutions are reasonably accessible.

If you’re evolving programs, for example, most random changes to a program aren’t going to make it smarter. So just running the same evolutionary algorithm a million times faster doesn’t necessarily get you to general intelligence. The representation matters, the fitness measure matters, and it matters how you reuse things you’ve already learned.

Where I get excited is combining evolutionary search with other kinds of learning and reasoning. You might have a neural network learn patterns that guide the evolutionary search, while a reasoning system supplies constraints or breaks a problem into pieces. Then evolution can discover things that neither system would readily come up with on its own.

So I wouldn’t dismiss an approach because it’s old. More computing power can make previously impractical ideas useful. But I think the path to AGI involves getting these different processes to work together, rather than expecting raw computation to solve all the architectural problems.
